item.question: A mat has 5 equal sides, and each side is 7 cm long. Grandmother wants to sew a lace all the way round its border. How long is the lace?
steps: The border is the line all the way round the mat, so we add the length of all 5 sides.
All the sides are equal, so we can also multiply: 5 sides of 7 cm make 5 × 7 = 35.
Check: adding and multiplying both give 35, so the lace must be 35 cm long.
item.answer: The perimeter is 35 cm, so the lace is 35 cm long

2. 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 35.

4. Check: adding and multiplying both give 35, so the lace must be 35 cm long.
Answer: The perimeter is 35 cm, so the lace is 35 cm long

steps_tex: The border is the line all the way round the quilt. Count one unit of lace for each patch side along it.
One long side has $15$ patches, so it needs $15\text{ units}$. One short side has $10$ patches, so it needs $10\text{ units}$.
The quilt has $2$ long sides and $2$ short sides: $15 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 50$.
The border is $50\text{ units}$ long.
Red lace is $40\text{ units}$ and $40$ is less than $50$, so it is too short. Blue lace is $25\text{ units}$ and $25$ is less than $50$, so it is too short.
Green lace is $50\text{ units}$, exactly the length of the border.

item.question: Grandmother wants to cover a tray top with identical tiles. She tries 12 square tiles in 3 rows of 4, and 6 round tiles in 2 rows of 3. Which tiles cover the tray with no gaps and no overlaps?
steps: Squares first: 3 rows of 4 squares, 3 × 4 = 12 squares.
The squares meet edge to edge, so there are no gaps and no overlaps: squares tile.
Now the round tiles: 2 rows of 3 circles, 2 × 3 = 6 circles.
There are gaps between the circles and at the corners of the tray. Pushing the circles together to close the gaps would make them overlap.
Check: only the squares cover the tray with no gaps and no overlaps.
item.answer: The square tiles cover the tray exactly; the round tiles leave gaps

Answer: The square tiles cover the tray exactly; the round tiles leave gaps

item.question: A tray top is covered by 24 square tiles in 4 rows of 6. Every square is then cut from corner to corner into 2 triangles, and the same tray top is covered with the triangles. What is the area of the tray top in square units and in triangle units?
steps: Count the squares: 4 rows of 6, 4 × 6 = 24 squares. The area is 24 square units.
Each square makes 2 triangles, so the triangles are 24 × 2 = 48.
The same tray top is covered by 48 triangles. The area is 48 triangle units.
The region did not change, only the tile did, so a different tile gives a different count.
Check: 48 ÷ 2 = 24, so 2 triangles make 1 square.
item.answer: The area is 24 square units, which is 48 triangle units

item.question: Now, try to cover the top of your table without gaps and overlaps with the following objects of same size. (a) Notebooks (b) Lunch boxes (c) Pencil boxes (d) Maths books. Which of the above objects covered the region completely?
steps_tex: Notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes and maths books are all rectangles. Rectangles tile: they fit side by side with no gaps and no overlaps.
So each of the four objects can cover a table top without gaps and overlaps if you lay it in neat rows.
Whether an object covers the table completely depends on the table: its length and breadth must hold a whole number of the objects.
Sample answer with practice values: a notebook $20\text{ cm}$ long and $15\text{ cm}$ broad, and a table top $60\text{ cm}$ long and $30\text{ cm}$ broad.
Along the length: $60 \div 20 = 3$ notebooks. Along the breadth: $30 \div 15 = 2$ notebooks.
$3 \times 2 = 6$ notebooks cover this table top completely.
Your answer may differ, because your table and your objects may be different sizes.
item.answer_tex: Sample answer: all four, because every one is a rectangle and rectangles tile. Your answer may differ.

Sample answer with practice values: a notebook 20 cm long and 15 cm broad, and a table top 60 cm long and 30 cm broad.

item.question: Mat P is 7 squares long and 2 squares broad. Mat Q is 4 squares long and 4 squares broad. Which mat has the larger area?
steps: Lay mat Q on mat P. Q is shorter than P in length, but Q is broader. Neither mat fits inside the other, so laying them does not settle it.
Cover both with the same square tiles and count. Mat P has 2 rows of 7 squares: 2 × 7 = 14 squares.
Mat Q has 4 rows of 4 squares: 4 × 4 = 16 squares.
16 is more than 14, so mat Q has the larger area.
Check: Q is not the longer mat, yet it has the larger area, so length alone cannot decide.
item.answer: Mat Q has the larger area: 16 squares is more than 14 squares

concept_name: The Unit Square and Counting Squares

item.question: A triangle is drawn on a grid of 1 cm squares. It covers 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. What is its area?
steps: The area of a square with sides 1 cm is 1 square cm, so each whole square counts 1 square cm.
Count the whole squares: 6 whole squares are 6 square cm.
Count the half squares: there are 4, and 2 half squares make 1 whole square, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2 whole squares.
Check: the 4 half squares match up in 2 pairs, so none is left over.
item.text:
Worked example: A triangle is drawn on a grid of 1 cm squares. It covers 6 whole squares and 4 half squares. What is its area?
1. The area of a square with sides 1 cm is 1 square cm, so each whole square counts 1 square cm.
2. Count the whole squares: 6 whole squares are 6 square cm.
3. Count the half squares: there are 4, and 2 half squares make 1 whole square, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2 whole squares.
4. Add: 6 + 2 = 8.
5. Check: the 4 half squares match up in 2 pairs, so none is left over.
Answer: The area is 8 square cm
